title: Inference
tagline: Decoding and sampling, the KV cache, batching, quantisation, speculative decoding and long context
summary: Every generated token costs time, memory and money. This course explains decoding and sampling strategies, the key–value cache, batching and memory management in serving systems, quantisation and distillation, speculative decoding, long-context inference, and how latency, throughput and cost trade off.
overview: A model is trained once and run billions of times. Inference is where most of a language model’s cost is paid, and its constraints differ from training: tokens are generated one at a time, each step reads the whole model and its cache from memory, and users notice every delay. This course explains how a model turns a prompt into text, and how serving systems make that fast and cheap.

It begins with decoding — greedy decoding, temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling — and the key–value cache that makes incremental decoding possible and whose memory grows with every token and every concurrent user. Serving systems batch requests continuously, manage cache memory in pages, and separate the compute-bound prefill phase from the memory-bound decode phase. Quantisation shrinks weights and caches to 8, 4 or fewer bits; distillation and pruning produce smaller models; speculative decoding lets a small draft model propose tokens that the large model checks in parallel. Long-context inference adds position interpolation and the attention sinks that keep streaming models stable, and the last chapter measures what users and operators care about: time to first token, tokens per second and cost per token.

Inference is limited by memory bandwidth more often than by arithmetic, so the key skill is to estimate bytes moved as well as FLOPs. Before optimising, measure: profile a realistic workload, find whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound, and only then choose a technique.
outcomes: Implement greedy decoding, temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling, and explain their effect on quality and diversity.
Calculate the memory of the key–value cache, and explain how multi-query and grouped-query attention reduce it.
Describe continuous batching, paged attention and the prefill and decode phases of serving.
Explain post-training quantisation of weights, activations and caches, and its effect on accuracy.
Compare distillation and structured and unstructured pruning for producing smaller models.
Show why speculative decoding preserves the target model’s output distribution, and estimate its speed-up.
Explain techniques for long-context inference, including position interpolation and attention sinks.
Measure and optimise time to first token, throughput and cost per token.

history.title: Nucleus sampling
history.detail: Holtzman and colleagues showed that sampling from the smallest set of tokens holding most of the probability avoids both the repetition of greedy decoding and the incoherence of pure sampling.

history.title: LLM.int8()
history.detail: Dettmers and colleagues found that a few outlier features break naive 8-bit quantisation of large models, and kept those features in higher precision.

history.title: GPTQ
history.detail: Frantar and colleagues quantised the weights of 175-billion-parameter models to 3 or 4 bits in a few GPU hours, using approximate second-order information.

history.title: Continuous batching
history.detail: Yu and colleagues’ Orca scheduled work one iteration at a time, letting new requests join a running batch as others finish.

history.title: Speculative decoding
history.detail: Leviathan, Kalman and Matias, and independently Chen and colleagues, used a small draft model to propose several tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, with an acceptance rule that leaves the output distribution unchanged.

history.title: PagedAttention
history.detail: Kwon and colleagues stored the key–value cache in fixed-size pages, as operating systems do with virtual memory, and built the vLLM serving system on the idea.

history.title: Position interpolation
history.detail: Chen and colleagues at Meta extended the context window of RoPE models by scaling positions down into the trained range, needing only brief fine-tuning.

history.title: Attention sinks
history.detail: Xiao and colleagues found that models place large attention on the first tokens, and that keeping those tokens in the cache lets a model generate stably far beyond its training length.
